questions.stem: The graph shows the velocity of a cart moving along a straight track. What is the displacement of the cart from \(t=0\) to \(t=8\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Displacement is the signed area under the graph. The velocity is zero at \(t=6.5\text{ s}\), so the area above the axis is \(6+18+4.5=28.5\text{ m}\) and the area below is \(4.5\text{ m}\), giving \(24\text{ m}\). The total distance traveled is \(33\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the velocity of a cart moving along a straight track. What is the acceleration of the cart at the instant its velocity is zero during the interval \(5\text{ s}<t<8\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph: \(\dfrac{-6-6}{8-5}=-4\text{ m/s}^2\). A velocity of zero does not mean the acceleration is zero; the slope is the same throughout the segment.

questions.stem: The graph shows the positions of carts A and B as functions of time. At which time, if any, do the two carts have the same speed?
choices: At no time, because cart B is always accelerating
questions.explanation: Speed is the slope of a position graph. Cart A has a constant slope of \(2\text{ m/s}\); the slope of cart B's curve equals \(2\text{ m/s}\) at \(t=2\text{ s}\). At \(t=4\text{ s}\) the carts are at the same position, but cart B is moving twice as fast.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at \(20\text{ m/s}\) from the edge of a cliff \(60\text{ m}\) above the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), how long after it is thrown does the ball reach the ground?
questions.explanation: Taking up as positive, \(-60=20t-5t^2\), so \(t^2-4t-12=0\) and \(t=6\text{ s}\). Four seconds is only the time to return to the launch height.

questions.stem: Balls A and B are thrown from the top of a cliff with the same initial speed, as shown. Ball A is thrown horizontally and ball B is thrown at an angle above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following correctly compares the balls when they reach the ground?
choices: They land with the same speed at the same time.
Ball B lands with a greater speed and lands later.
Ball A lands with a greater speed and lands earlier.
They land with the same speed, and ball B lands later.
questions.explanation: Both balls start with the same kinetic energy and fall through the same height, so they gain the same kinetic energy and land with equal speeds. Ball B has an upward initial velocity component, so it spends more time in the air.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched from level ground at \(30\text{ m/s}\) at an angle of \(53^\circ\) above the horizontal \((\sin 53^\circ=0.8,\ \cos 53^\circ=0.6)\). Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\) and neglecting air resistance, how far has the projectile traveled horizontally when it reaches its maximum height?
questions.explanation: The vertical velocity component is \(24\text{ m/s}\), so the time to the top is \(2.4\text{ s}\). The horizontal component is \(18\text{ m/s}\), giving \(18(2.4)=43.2\text{ m}\). The maximum height is \(28.8\text{ m}\) and the full range is \(86.4\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up and returns to the height from which it was thrown. Air resistance is not negligible. How does the time the ball takes to rise compare with the time it takes to fall back?
choices: The rise takes longer, because the ball is moving faster on the way up.
The two times are equal, because the ball covers the same distance each way.
The fall takes longer, because the ball's average speed is smaller on the way down.
The two times are equal, because air resistance acts in both directions.
questions.explanation: On the way up, gravity and air resistance both act downward, so the ball slows quickly. On the way down they oppose each other, so the ball speeds up slowly and has lost mechanical energy. At every height the ball is slower coming down than going up, so the same distance takes more time.

questions.stem: Car A travels at a constant \(20\text{ m/s}\). At the instant it passes car B, which is at rest, car B begins to accelerate at a constant \(4\text{ m/s}^2\) in the same direction. What is the speed of car B at the instant it catches up with car A?
questions.explanation: The cars are side by side when \(20t=\tfrac{1}{2}(4)t^2\), so \(t=10\text{ s}\) and car B's speed is \(4(10)=40\text{ m/s}\). To cover the same distance in the same time from rest, car B must end at twice car A's constant speed.

questions.stem: Students drop a ball from rest from several heights \(h\) and measure the fall time \(t\) for each. Which graph of their data should be a straight line whose slope equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}g\)?
questions.explanation: Because \(h=\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2\), plotting \(h\) against \(t^2\) gives a line of slope \(\tfrac{1}{2}g\). A graph of \(\sqrt{h}\) against \(t\) is also linear, but its slope is \(\sqrt{g/2}\).

questions.stem: A boat moves at \(5\text{ m/s}\) relative to the water in a river that flows at \(3\text{ m/s}\). The river is \(100\text{ m}\) wide. If the boat is steered so that it travels straight across to the point directly opposite its starting point, how long does the crossing take?
questions.explanation: The boat must point partly upstream so that \(3\text{ m/s}\) of its velocity cancels the current. The remaining component across the river is \(\sqrt{5^2-3^2}=4\text{ m/s}\), so the time is \(100/4=25\text{ s}\). Twenty seconds is the time if the boat points straight across and is carried downstream.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal table of height \(h\) with speed \(v\) and lands a horizontal distance \(d\) from the table. If the ball instead leaves a table of height \(4h\) with speed \(2v\), how far from the table does it land?
questions.explanation: The fall time is \(\sqrt{2h/g}\), so quadrupling the height doubles the time. The horizontal distance is speed times time, so doubling both gives \(4d\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the velocity of a cart moving along a straight track. During which time interval is the speed of the cart decreasing?
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of velocity. From \(5\text{ s}\) to \(6.5\text{ s}\) the velocity is positive and approaching zero, so the cart slows. After \(6.5\text{ s}\) the velocity is negative and growing in magnitude, so the cart speeds up even though the graph is still falling.

questions.stem: The graph shows the positions of carts A and B as functions of time. How do the average velocities of the carts compare for the interval from \(t=0\) to \(t=4\text{ s}\)?
choices: They are equal, because the carts have the same displacement in the same time.
Cart A's is greater, because cart B moves slowly for most of the interval.
Cart B's is greater, because cart B is moving faster at the end of the interval.
They cannot be compared, because cart B is accelerating.
questions.explanation: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time. Both carts start at \(x=0\) and are at \(x=8\text{ m}\) at \(t=4\text{ s}\), so their average velocities are both \(2\text{ m/s}\), whatever happens in between.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown at an angle above the horizontal and air resistance is negligible. Which of the following describes the angle between the ball's velocity vector and its acceleration vector during the flight?
choices: It is \(180^\circ\) while the ball rises and \(0^\circ\) while the ball falls.
It is less than \(90^\circ\) while the ball rises and greater than \(90^\circ\) while the ball falls.
It is greater than \(90^\circ\) while the ball rises, \(90^\circ\) at the top, and less than \(90^\circ\) while the ball falls.
questions.explanation: The acceleration always points straight down. While the ball rises its velocity has an upward component, so the angle between the vectors exceeds \(90^\circ\) and the ball slows. At the top the velocity is horizontal. While the ball falls the velocity has a downward component and the ball speeds up.

questions.stem: A dart is aimed directly at a target hanging from a tree. At the instant the dart is fired, the target is released and falls from rest. Air resistance is negligible, and the dart is fast enough to reach the target's horizontal position before either hits the ground. Which of the following is true?
choices: The dart passes above the target, because the target has been falling for the whole time.
The dart hits the target, because both fall the same distance below the straight line along which the dart was aimed.
The dart passes below the target, because the dart's upward speed decreases while the target simply falls.
Whether the dart hits depends on the dart's launch speed.
questions.explanation: Without gravity the dart would travel along its aiming line and strike the stationary target. With gravity, in any time \(t\) both the dart and the target are displaced downward by the same amount, \(\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2\), from where they would otherwise be, so they still meet.

questions.stem: An object moves along a straight line. At \(t=0\) its velocity is in the \(+x\) direction, and its acceleration is constant and in the \(-x\) direction for all later times. Which of the following describes the object's motion?
choices: It slows, stops, and then remains at rest.
It slows, stops for an instant, and then speeds up in the \(-x\) direction.
It slows but never stops, because the acceleration is constant.
It continues in the \(+x\) direction at a decreasing speed for all later times.
questions.explanation: A constant acceleration changes the velocity at a steady rate, so the velocity decreases through zero and becomes negative. The object is at rest only for an instant; the acceleration does not vanish when the velocity does.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) slides down a ramp inclined at angle \(\theta\), as shown. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the ramp is \(\mu_k\). What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?
questions.explanation: Along the ramp, \(mg\sin\theta-\mu_kN=ma\). Perpendicular to the ramp, \(N=mg\cos\theta\). Substituting gives \(a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)\).

questions.stem: A block rests on a rough ramp, as shown. The angle \(\theta\) of the ramp is slowly increased, and the block remains at rest. How do the magnitudes of the normal force and the friction force on the block change as \(\theta\) increases?
choices: The normal force decreases and the friction force increases.
The normal force decreases and the friction force decreases.
The normal force stays the same and the friction force increases.
Both forces stay the same, because the block remains at rest.
questions.explanation: For a block at rest, \(N=mg\cos\theta\) and the static friction force equals \(mg\sin\theta\). As \(\theta\) increases, \(\cos\theta\) decreases and \(\sin\theta\) increases. Static friction equals \(\mu_sN\) only at the point of slipping.

In trial 1 the table is frictionless and the blocks accelerate. In trial 2 the table is rough and the blocks remain at rest. How does the tension in the string compare in the two trials?

The tension is the same, because the same block hangs from the string.
The tension is zero in trial 2, because nothing moves.
The tension is greater in trial 2.
questions.explanation: In trial 2 the hanging block is in equilibrium, so the tension equals \(m_2g\). In trial 1 the hanging block accelerates downward, so the net force on it is downward and the tension must be less than \(m_2g\).

It is kinetic friction directed to the left.

questions.stem: A ball of mass \(m\) on a string moves in a vertical circle, as shown. The only forces on the ball are gravity and the tension in the string. How much greater is the tension when the ball is at the bottom of the circle than when it is at the top?
questions.explanation: At the top, \(T_t+mg=\dfrac{mv_t^2}{R}\); at the bottom, \(T_b-mg=\dfrac{mv_b^2}{R}\). Energy conservation gives \(v_b^2=v_t^2+4gR\). Subtracting, \(T_b-T_t=2mg+4mg=6mg\), whatever the speed.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) around a planet with period \(T\). What is the period of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(2r\) around the same planet?
questions.explanation: Setting the gravitational force equal to \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\) gives \(T^2\propto r^3\). Doubling the radius multiplies \(T^2\) by 8, so the period becomes \(2\sqrt{2}\,T\).

questions.stem: A planet has twice the mass of Earth and half the radius of Earth. In terms of \(g\), the gravitational field strength at Earth's surface, what is the gravitational field strength at the surface of the planet?
questions.explanation: The surface field is \(\dfrac{GM}{R^2}\). Doubling \(M\) doubles the field, and halving \(R\) multiplies it by 4, for a total factor of 8.

questions.stem: A student stands on a scale in an elevator that is moving upward and slowing down. How does the reading on the scale compare with the student's weight, and why?
choices: It is greater than the weight, because the elevator is moving upward.
It is less than the weight, because the student's acceleration is downward.
It is equal to the weight, because the scale always measures the gravitational force.
It is greater than the weight, because the student's acceleration is upward.
questions.explanation: The scale reads the normal force. An object moving upward while slowing has a downward acceleration, so the net force is downward and the normal force is smaller than the gravitational force. The direction of motion alone does not determine the reading.

questions.stem: A car of mass \(m\) travels over the top of a hill whose cross section is a circular arc of radius \(r\). The speed of the car at the top is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{gr}\). What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the car by the road at the top of the hill?
questions.explanation: At the top the centripetal acceleration is downward, so \(mg-N=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{1}{4}mg\) and \(N=\dfrac{3}{4}mg\). The car would lose contact with the road at a speed of \(\sqrt{gr}\).

It is greater in trial 1, because the force is applied to the more massive block.
It is the same, because the acceleration of the blocks is the same in both trials.
It is the same, because the blocks exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
questions.explanation: The blocks have the same acceleration in both trials. In trial 1 the contact force is the net force on the lighter block B; in trial 2 it is the net force on the heavier block A, so it must be larger. Newton's third law relates the two forces within a single trial, not across trials.

questions.stem: A truck pushes a stalled car along a level road, and both vehicles are speeding up. How does the magnitude of the force the truck exerts on the car compare with the magnitude of the force the car exerts on the truck?
choices: The truck's force is greater, because the vehicles are speeding up.
The truck's force is greater, because the truck has more mass.
They are equal, even though the vehicles are accelerating.
The car's force is greater, because the car resists being moved.
questions.explanation: The two forces are a Newton's third law pair, so they are equal in magnitude under all conditions. The car speeds up because the truck's push exceeds the other forces on the car, not because it exceeds the car's push on the truck.

questions.stem: Blocks of mass \(m\) and \(3m\) hang from a light string over a light, frictionless pulley, as shown, and are released. The experiment is repeated with the \(3m\) block removed and a student pulling down on that end of the string with a constant force equal to \(3mg\). How does the acceleration of the block of mass \(m\) compare in the two cases?
choices: It is the same, because the same force acts on that end of the string.
It is smaller when the student pulls, because a hand cannot fall freely.
It is the same, because the block of mass \(m\) is unchanged.
It is greater when the student pulls, because the tension is then \(3mg\) instead of less than \(3mg\).
questions.explanation: With the hanging block, the \(3m\) block must itself accelerate downward, so the tension is less than its weight (it is \(\tfrac{3}{2}mg\)), and the small block accelerates at \(\tfrac{g}{2}\). When the student pulls with \(3mg\), the tension is \(3mg\) and the small block accelerates at \(2g\).

questions.stem: Astronauts in a space station orbiting Earth appear to float. Which of the following best explains why?
choices: The gravitational force on the astronauts is zero at the altitude of the station.
The gravitational force on the astronauts is balanced by an outward centrifugal force.
The astronauts and the station are both in free fall, accelerating toward Earth at the same rate.
The station's walls shield the astronauts from Earth's gravitational field.
questions.explanation: At the altitude of a typical station the gravitational field is only slightly weaker than at the surface, and gravity is what keeps the station in orbit. Because the astronauts and the station share the same acceleration, the station exerts no normal force on them.

questions.explanation: The net work is the area under the graph. questions.stem: The graph shows the net force on an object as a function of its position. The object is at rest at \(x=0\). Which of the following describes the motion of the object between \(x=4\text{ m}\) and \(x=6\text{ m}\)?
choices: It is speeding up, and its acceleration is decreasing in magnitude.
It is slowing down, because the force is decreasing.
It is moving at constant speed, because the force is changing at a constant rate.
It is speeding up, and its acceleration is increasing in magnitude.
questions.explanation: The net force is still positive in this interval, so it continues to do positive work and the object speeds up. Because the force is getting smaller, the acceleration is getting smaller. The object does not begin to slow until the force becomes negative beyond \(x=6\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: A block is released from rest at the top of a rough ramp of height \(h\) inclined at angle \(\theta\), as shown. The coefficient of kinetic friction is \(\mu_k\). What is the speed of the block at the bottom of the ramp?
questions.explanation: The ramp has length \(\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}\) and the friction force is \(\mu_kmg\cos\theta\), so the energy dissipated is \(\dfrac{\mu_kmgh}{\tan\theta}\). Then \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2=mgh-\dfrac{\mu_kmgh}{\tan\theta}\).

questions.stem: A small block is released from rest at height \(h\) on a frictionless track that includes a vertical loop of radius \(R\), as shown. What is the minimum value of \(h\) for which the block stays in contact with the track at the top of the loop?
questions.explanation: At the top, contact is just maintained when gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: \(mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\), so \(v^2=gR\). Energy conservation gives \(mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac{1}{2}mgR\), so \(h=\dfrac{5}{2}R\).

questions.stem: A small block is released from rest at height \(h=2R\) on a frictionless track that includes a vertical loop of radius \(R\), as shown. Which of the following describes what happens to the block?
choices: It reaches the top of the loop with zero speed and then falls straight down.
It travels around the entire loop, because it starts at the height of the top of the loop.
It stops at the height of the loop's center and slides back down.
It loses contact with the track at a point between the height of the loop's center and the top of the loop.
questions.explanation: Energy conservation would allow the block to reach height \(2R\) only with zero speed, but staying on the track at the top requires a speed of at least \(\sqrt{gR}\). The normal force therefore reaches zero before the top, and the block leaves the track as a projectile while still moving.

questions.stem: A spring compressed a distance \(x\) launches a block from rest up a frictionless ramp, and the block rises to a maximum height \(h\) above its starting point. If the spring is instead compressed a distance \(3x\), to what maximum height does the block rise?
questions.explanation: All of the spring's energy becomes gravitational potential energy: \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2=mgh\). The stored energy depends on the square of the compression, so tripling it gives nine times the height.

questions.stem: A car starts from rest on a level road, and its engine delivers constant power to the wheels. Resistive forces are negligible. Which of the following describes the car's motion?
choices: Its acceleration decreases as its speed increases.
Its acceleration increases as its speed increases.
Its speed is constant, because the power is constant.
questions.explanation: Power is \(P=Fv\), so with constant power the driving force is \(\dfrac{P}{v}\), which shrinks as the speed grows. Equivalently, kinetic energy increases in proportion to time, so the speed is proportional to \(\sqrt{t}\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U\) of a system as a function of the position \(x\) of an object in the system. The total mechanical energy of the system is \(E=6\text{ J}\). Which of the following describes the object's motion?
choices: It moves back and forth between \(x=0\) and \(x=4\text{ m}\), moving fastest at those end points.
It comes to rest at \(x=2\text{ m}\), where the potential energy is zero.
It moves in the \(+x\) direction indefinitely, because its total energy is greater than zero.
It moves back and forth between about \(x=0.3\text{ m}\) and \(x=3.7\text{ m}\), moving fastest at \(x=2\text{ m}\).
questions.explanation: The kinetic energy is \(E-U\), which is zero where the curve meets the dashed line and greatest where \(U\) is smallest. The object cannot enter regions where \(U\) would exceed \(E\), so it turns around near \(x=0.3\text{ m}\) and \(x=3.7\text{ m}\).

figure.alt: Potential energy versus position graph: a parabola with minimum 0 J at x = 2 m, rising to 8 J at x = 0 m and x = 4 m. A dashed horizontal line marks total mechanical energy E = 6 J

questions.stem: The graph shows the potential energy \(U\) of a system as a function of the position \(x\) of an object in the system; the curve is \(U=2(x-2)^2\) with \(U\) in joules and \(x\) in meters. What force is exerted on the object when it is at \(x=3\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: The force is the negative of the slope of the potential energy graph. At \(x=3\text{ m}\) the slope is \(4(3-2)=4\text{ J/m}\), so the force is \(4\text{ N}\) toward decreasing \(x\), back toward the minimum. The value \(2\text{ J}\) is the potential energy there, not the force.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) is pressed against a spring of spring constant \(k\), compressing it a distance \(x\), and released from rest. After leaving the spring, the block slides across a rough horizontal surface with coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k\). How far does the block slide on the rough surface before stopping?
questions.explanation: The spring's energy is entirely dissipated by friction: \(\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2=\mu_kmgd\), so \(d=\dfrac{kx^2}{2\mu_kmg}\).

questions.stem: A block slides down a frictionless ramp. Students analyze the motion using a system that consists of the block alone. Which of the following is a correct statement about that system?
choices: No work is done on the system, and its gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy.
The normal force does positive work on the system, increasing its kinetic energy.
The total mechanical energy of the system stays constant.
Earth does positive work on the system, increasing its kinetic energy; the system has no gravitational potential energy.
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy belongs to a system of interacting objects, so a single block has none. With the block as the system, Earth's gravitational force is external and does positive work. The description in terms of potential energy applies to the block–Earth system.

questions.stem: A pendulum bob of mass \(m\) on a string is released from rest with the string horizontal. What is the tension in the string when the bob passes through the lowest point of its swing?
questions.explanation: Falling through the string length \(L\) gives \(v^2=2gL\). At the bottom, \(T-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{L}=2mg\), so \(T=3mg\).

questions.stem: A \(1.0\text{ kg}\) block is dropped from rest from \(0.20\text{ m}\) above the top of a vertical spring with spring constant \(200\text{ N/m}\). Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is the maximum compression of the spring?
questions.explanation: The block falls a total distance \(0.20+x\) before stopping, so \(mg(0.20+x)=\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2\), or \(100x^2-10x-2=0\), which gives \(x=0.20\text{ m}\). Ignoring the extra distance \(x\) gives \(0.14\text{ m}\), and \(0.05\text{ m}\) is the compression at which the block would sit in equilibrium.

questions.stem: A block slides from rest down the rough ramp shown and reaches the bottom with speed \(v\). The ramp is replaced with a steeper one of the same height \(h\) and the same coefficient of kinetic friction. How does the block's speed at the bottom of the steeper ramp compare with \(v\)?
choices: It is greater, because both the friction force and the distance over which it acts are smaller.
It is the same, because the block descends through the same height.
It is smaller, because the block has less time to speed up.
It is the same, because the coefficient of friction is the same.
questions.explanation: The energy dissipated by friction is \(\mu_kmg\cos\theta\) multiplied by the ramp length \(\dfrac{h}{\sin\theta}\), which equals \(\dfrac{\mu_kmgh}{\tan\theta}\). A steeper ramp makes this smaller, so more of the potential energy becomes kinetic energy. Only without friction would the speeds be equal.

questions.stem: A small block slides along the frictionless track shown and travels all the way around the loop. At which point in the loop is the normal force exerted on the block by the track greatest?
choices: At the top of the loop
At the points level with the center of the loop
At the bottom of the loop
It is the same at every point, because the track is frictionless.
questions.explanation: At the bottom the block is moving fastest, so it needs the largest centripetal force, and the normal force must also overcome gravity: \(N=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}+mg\). At the top the speed is least and gravity helps supply the centripetal force, so the normal force is smallest there.

questions.stem: A crate rests on the bed of a truck. The truck speeds up along a level road, and the crate does not slide on the bed. In the reference frame of the road, which of the following is true of the static friction force exerted on the crate by the truck bed?
choices: It does positive work on the crate, because it acts in the direction of the crate's displacement.
It does no work on the crate, because static friction never does work.
It does negative work on the crate, because friction opposes motion.
It does no work on the crate, because the crate does not move relative to the truck bed.
questions.explanation: The crate's kinetic energy increases, and static friction is the only horizontal force on it, so that force does positive work. Static friction opposes relative sliding between surfaces, not motion itself, and the crate is displaced relative to the road while the force acts.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from rest and air resistance is negligible. Which of the following describes a graph of the ball's kinetic energy as a function of the distance it has fallen?
choices: A parabola that opens upward, because the ball's speed increases
A horizontal line, because mechanical energy is conserved
A curve that levels off as the ball approaches the ground
A straight line through the origin with slope \(mg\)
questions.explanation: The work done by gravity is \(mg\) multiplied by the distance fallen, and that work equals the kinetic energy gained, so the graph is linear. Plotted against time instead, the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}mg^2t^2\), which is a parabola.

Cart X has more momentum and more kinetic energy.

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation gives a final speed of \(\dfrac{2}{3}v\). The final kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(3m)\left(\tfrac{2}{3}v\right)^2=\tfrac{2}{3}mv^2\), which is two thirds of the initial \(mv^2\), so one third is dissipated.

choices: The lighter cart moves left at \(\dfrac{v}{2}\) and the heavier cart moves right at \(\dfrac{v}{2}\).
The lighter cart stops and the heavier cart moves right at \(\dfrac{v}{3}\).
The lighter cart moves left at \(v\) and the heavier cart moves right at \(\dfrac{2v}{3}\).
questions.explanation: These velocities conserve momentum, \(mv=-\tfrac{1}{2}mv+\tfrac{3}{2}mv\), and kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2=\tfrac{1}{8}mv^2+\tfrac{3}{8}mv^2\). The other choices conserve momentum at most; the last one would create kinetic energy.

questions.stem: A \(1\text{ kg}\) cart moving at \(4\text{ m/s}\) in the \(+x\) direction collides with a \(3\text{ kg}\) cart at rest on a level, frictionless track. Which of the following pairs of velocities after the collision is NOT physically possible?
choices: \(1\text{ kg}\) cart: \(-2\text{ m/s}\); \(3\text{ kg}\) cart: \(+2\text{ m/s}\)
\(1\text{ kg}\) cart: \(+1\text{ m/s}\); \(3\text{ kg}\) cart: \(+1\text{ m/s}\)
\(1\text{ kg}\) cart: \(-3\text{ m/s}\); \(3\text{ kg}\) cart: \(+\tfrac{7}{3}\text{ m/s}\)
\(1\text{ kg}\) cart: \(-1\text{ m/s}\); \(3\text{ kg}\) cart: \(+\tfrac{5}{3}\text{ m/s}\)
questions.explanation: Every pair conserves the initial momentum of \(4\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}\). The initial kinetic energy is \(8\text{ J}\). The pair with \(-3\text{ m/s}\) and \(\tfrac{7}{3}\text{ m/s}\) has about \(12.7\text{ J}\), more than the carts started with, which a collision cannot produce. The others have \(8\text{ J}\), \(2\text{ J}\), and about \(4.7\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: A firework shell is launched at an angle and explodes into many pieces at the top of its path. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following describes the motion of the center of mass of the pieces after the explosion, before any piece lands?
choices: It falls straight down from the point of the explosion.
It remains at rest at the point of the explosion.
It moves horizontally at constant velocity.
It continues along the same parabolic path the shell was following.
questions.explanation: The explosion involves only forces internal to the system of pieces, so it cannot change the motion of the center of mass. The only external force is still gravity, so the center of mass continues along the original parabola.

questions.stem: A \(3\text{ kg}\) object at rest explodes into a \(1\text{ kg}\) piece and a \(2\text{ kg}\) piece that move apart in opposite directions. The explosion gives the pieces a total kinetic energy of \(60\text{ J}\). What is the kinetic energy of the \(1\text{ kg}\) piece?
questions.explanation: The pieces have momenta of equal magnitude \(p\). Because kinetic energy is \(\dfrac{p^2}{2m}\), the piece with half the mass has twice the kinetic energy, so the energy divides as \(40\text{ J}\) and \(20\text{ J}\).

questions.stem: A person of mass \(m\) stands at one end of a boat of mass \(3m\) and length \(L\) that is at rest in still water. The person walks to the other end of the boat. Neglecting any resistance from the water, how far does the boat move relative to the water?
questions.explanation: With no external horizontal force, the center of mass of the person–boat system stays in place. If the boat moves a distance \(d\) one way, the person moves \(L-d\) the other way relative to the water, so \(m(L-d)=3md\) and \(d=\dfrac{L}{4}\).

questions.stem: A car of mass \(2m\) traveling east at speed \(v\) collides with a car of mass \(m\) traveling north at speed \(2v\). The cars stick together. What is their speed immediately after the collision?
questions.explanation: Each car has momentum of magnitude \(2mv\), one east and one north, so the total momentum has magnitude \(2\sqrt{2}\,mv\). Dividing by the combined mass \(3m\) gives \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}v\). Adding the momenta as if they were in the same direction gives \(\dfrac{4}{3}v\).

questions.stem: A rubber ball and a lump of clay have the same mass and are thrown at the same speed at a door that is free to swing. The ball bounces back; the clay sticks. Which object is more likely to make the door swing, and why?
choices: The clay, because it transfers all of its momentum to the door.
The clay, because it stays in contact with the door for a longer time.
The ball, because its momentum changes by a greater amount, so it delivers a greater impulse to the door.
Neither is more likely, because they strike the door with the same momentum.
questions.explanation: The clay's momentum changes from \(mv\) to nearly zero, while the ball's changes from \(mv\) to nearly \(-mv\), about twice as much. By Newton's third law the door receives an equal and opposite impulse, so the ball delivers roughly twice the impulse.

questions.stem: A bullet of mass \(m\) is fired horizontally into a block of mass \(M\) hanging at rest from long strings. The bullet becomes embedded, and the block swings upward to a maximum height \(h\) above its starting position. What was the speed of the bullet just before it hit the block?
questions.explanation: After the collision, energy conservation gives the combined speed \(V=\sqrt{2gh}\). During the collision only momentum is conserved: \(mv=(m+M)V\). Applying energy conservation to the whole process ignores the energy dissipated as the bullet embeds.

questions.stem: Two carts on a level, frictionless track are held together with a compressed spring between them and then released from rest. Which of the following is true as the spring expands, for the system named?
choices: For the system of both carts and the spring, the total momentum and the total kinetic energy both remain zero.
For a system consisting of one cart alone, the momentum of the system is constant.
For the system of both carts and the spring, the total momentum increases as the carts speed up.
For the system of both carts and the spring, the total momentum remains zero while the total kinetic energy increases.
questions.explanation: No net external force acts on the two carts and spring together, so their total momentum stays at zero: the carts gain equal and opposite momenta. Kinetic energy increases as the spring's potential energy is converted. A single cart is acted on by the external spring force, so its momentum changes.

questions.stem: A ball of mass \(m\) is dropped from rest from height \(h\), hits the floor, and rebounds to a maximum height of \(\dfrac{h}{4}\). What is the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the ball by the floor? Neglect the impulse of gravity during the brief contact.
questions.explanation: The ball arrives with speed \(\sqrt{2gh}\) downward and leaves with speed \(\sqrt{2g(h/4)}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2gh}\) upward. Because the direction reverses, the change in momentum is the sum of the two magnitudes, \(\dfrac{3}{2}m\sqrt{2gh}\).

questions.stem: A cart of mass \(2m\) collides with a cart of mass \(m\) that is at rest, as shown. Which of the following correctly compares the two carts during the collision?
choices: The heavier cart exerts the greater force, and the lighter cart has the greater acceleration.
The forces on the carts have equal magnitudes, and the lighter cart has the greater acceleration.
The forces on the carts have equal magnitudes, and the accelerations have equal magnitudes.
The moving cart exerts the greater force, because the other cart is at rest.
questions.explanation: The forces the carts exert on each other are a Newton's third law pair and are equal at every instant. Because acceleration is force divided by mass, the cart with half the mass has twice the acceleration.

questions.stem: The graph shows the net force exerted on a cart as a function of time. During which time interval is the cart's momentum changing at the greatest rate?
choices: From \(t=0\) to \(t=2\text{ s}\), because the force is increasing
From \(t=4\text{ s}\) to \(t=6\text{ s}\), because the cart is moving fastest
The rate is the same throughout, because the force acts in one direction
questions.explanation: The rate of change of momentum equals the net force, so it is greatest when the force is greatest, which is between \(2\text{ s}\) and \(4\text{ s}\). How quickly the force itself is changing does not determine how quickly the momentum changes.

questions.stem: An open cart rolls along a level, frictionless track. In case 1, rain falling vertically collects in the cart. In case 2, there is no rain and water already in the cart drains straight down through a hole in its floor. How does the speed of the cart change in each case?
choices: It decreases in case 1 and stays the same in case 2.
It decreases in case 1 and increases in case 2.
It stays the same in both cases, because no horizontal force acts on the cart.
It stays the same in case 1 and increases in case 2.
questions.explanation: Falling rain has no horizontal momentum, so the cart must share its momentum with the added water and slows down. Draining water leaves with the same horizontal velocity as the cart, carrying away its own share of the momentum, so nothing changes the speed of what remains.

questions.stem: A rubber ball strikes a wall that is fixed to the ground and bounces straight back with the same speed. A student claims that momentum is not conserved because the ball's momentum changed. Which of the following correctly evaluates the claim?
choices: The claim is incorrect, because the ball's momentum has the same magnitude before and after the collision.
The claim is correct, because momentum is conserved only when kinetic energy is lost.
The momentum of the ball alone is not constant, but the momentum of the ball–wall–Earth system is conserved.
The claim is correct, because the wall does not move.
questions.explanation: The wall exerts an external force on the ball, so the momentum of the ball alone changes by \(2mv\). The wall and Earth receive an equal and opposite change in momentum; because their mass is enormous, the resulting change in their velocity is far too small to notice.

questions.stem: A uniform plank of length \(L\) and mass \(M\) rests on a pivot located \(\dfrac{L}{4}\) from its left end. A block of mass \(m\) placed at the left end keeps the plank balanced horizontally, as shown. What is \(m\) in terms of \(M\)?
questions.explanation: The plank's weight acts at its center, which is \(\dfrac{L}{4}\) to the right of the pivot. The block is \(\dfrac{L}{4}\) to the left. Equal lever arms require equal weights, so \(m=M\). Treating the plank's weight as acting at its right end gives an incorrect result.

Away from the wall, because the cable pulls the rod toward the wall.

It cannot be determined without knowing the masses of the rod and the sign.

questions.stem: A string wrapped around a uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) supports a hanging block of mass \(m\), as shown. The disk turns on a frictionless axle, and its rotational inertia is \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\). The block is released from rest. What is the magnitude of the block's acceleration?
questions.explanation: For the block, \(mg-T=ma\). For the disk, \(TR=\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\alpha\) with \(a=R\alpha\), so \(T=\tfrac{1}{2}Ma\). Adding gives \(mg=\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}M\right)a\), so \(a=\dfrac{2mg}{2m+M}\).

questions.stem: A string wrapped around a uniform disk supports a hanging block, as shown, and the block is released from rest. The experiment is repeated with a disk of the same radius but greater mass. How do the block's acceleration and the tension in the string compare with the first trial?
choices: The acceleration is smaller and the tension is smaller.
The acceleration is the same and the tension is greater.
Both are the same, because the same block exerts the same force.
The acceleration is smaller and the tension is greater.
questions.explanation: A disk with more rotational inertia has a smaller angular acceleration for a given torque, so the block's acceleration decreases. For the block, \(T=m(g-a)\), so a smaller acceleration means a tension closer to the block's weight.

questions.stem: A door of width \(L\) is hinged along one edge. In case 1, a force of magnitude \(F\) is applied at the edge farthest from the hinges, perpendicular to the door. In case 2, a force of magnitude \(2F\) is applied at the middle of the door at an angle of \(30^\circ\) to the plane of the door. What is the ratio of the torque about the hinges in case 1 to that in case 2?
questions.explanation: In case 1 the torque is \(FL\). In case 2 it is \(2F\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)\sin 30^\circ=\dfrac{FL}{2}\). Only the component of a force perpendicular to the door contributes to the torque.

questions.stem: A uniform rod is free to rotate about an axis through its center. A force \(F\) applied perpendicular to the rod at one end gives it angular acceleration \(\alpha\). The axis is then moved to one end of the rod, and the same force is applied perpendicular to the rod at the other end. The rotational inertia of a rod is \(\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2\) about its center and \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\) about one end. What is the new angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: Moving the axis doubles the lever arm of the force, from \(\dfrac{L}{2}\) to \(L\), so the torque doubles. The rotational inertia becomes four times as large. The angular acceleration is \(\dfrac{\tau}{I}\), which changes by a factor of \(\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

questions.stem: A uniform ladder leans against a frictionless vertical wall, making an angle \(\theta\) with a rough horizontal floor. What is the minimum coefficient of static friction between the ladder and the floor for which the ladder does not slip?
questions.explanation: The floor's normal force equals the ladder's weight \(W\), and friction \(f\) balances the wall's normal force \(N_w\). Torques about the base give \(N_wL\sin\theta=W\dfrac{L}{2}\cos\theta\), so \(f=\dfrac{W}{2\tan\theta}\). Requiring \(f\le\mu_sW\) gives \(\mu_s\ge\dfrac{1}{2\tan\theta}\).

questions.stem: A heavier child and a lighter child sit on opposite sides of a seesaw, positioned so that it balances horizontally. Each child then moves the same distance \(d\) toward the pivot. What happens to the seesaw?
choices: The lighter child's side goes down, because the heavier child's torque decreases by a greater amount.
It stays balanced, because both children moved the same distance.
The heavier child's side goes down, because that child still exerts the greater force.
It stays balanced, because the ratio of the children's weights has not changed.
questions.explanation: Each child's torque decreases by that child's weight multiplied by \(d\). The heavier child loses more torque, so the lighter child's torque is now the larger one. The seesaw would stay balanced only if each distance were reduced by the same fraction.

questions.stem: A string is wrapped around a uniform solid cylinder of mass \(m\), and the free end of the string is held fixed. The cylinder is released from rest and falls vertically as the string unwinds without slipping. The rotational inertia of the cylinder is \(\tfrac{1}{2}mR^2\). What is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation: For translation, \(mg-T=ma\). For rotation about the center, \(TR=\tfrac{1}{2}mR^2\alpha\) with \(a=R\alpha\), so \(T=\tfrac{1}{2}ma\). Then \(mg=\tfrac{3}{2}ma\), so \(a=\tfrac{2}{3}g\) and \(T=\tfrac{1}{3}mg\).

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal beam that weighs \(40\text{ N}\) is supported by a scale under each end. A block that weighs \(80\text{ N}\) rests on the beam one fourth of the beam's length from the left end. What is the reading on the left scale?
questions.explanation: Taking torques about the right end for a beam of length \(L\): \(F_{\text{left}}L=40\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)+80\left(\dfrac{3L}{4}\right)\), so \(F_{\text{left}}=20+60=80\text{ N}\). The right scale reads the remaining \(40\text{ N}\).

questions.stem: A block at the left end of a uniform plank keeps the plank balanced on the pivot, as shown. The block is then moved a short distance to the right, toward the pivot. What happens to the plank?
choices: It rotates so that its left end moves down, because the block is closer to the pivot.
It stays balanced, because the weights of the block and the plank have not changed.
It rotates so that its right end moves down, because the block's torque is now smaller than the torque due to the plank's weight.
It stays balanced, because the pivot force increases to compensate.
questions.explanation: The plank's weight acts at its center, to the right of the pivot, and its torque is unchanged. Moving the block toward the pivot shortens its lever arm and reduces its torque, so the net torque rotates the right end downward. The pivot force acts at the pivot and exerts no torque about it.

questions.stem: Two blocks of different mass hang from the ends of a string that passes over a pulley. The pulley has significant mass and turns on a frictionless axle, and the string does not slip on the pulley. While the blocks are accelerating, how do the tensions in the two sides of the string compare?
choices: The tensions are equal, because it is a single string.
The tension is greater on the side of the heavier block, because a net torque is needed to give the pulley angular acceleration.
The tension is greater on the side of the lighter block, because that block is accelerating upward.
The tensions are equal, because the axle is frictionless.
questions.explanation: The pulley has rotational inertia and is speeding up, so the two tensions must exert unequal torques on it. The pulley turns toward the heavier block, so the tension on that side is larger. The tensions are equal only when the pulley's mass is negligible.

questions.stem: A rod lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface. Two forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction are then applied perpendicular to the rod, one at each end, and they remain perpendicular to the rod as it moves. Which of the following describes the motion of the rod?
choices: Its center of mass remains at rest and it rotates with increasing angular speed.
Its center of mass accelerates and it does not rotate.
It remains at rest, because the forces cancel.
Its center of mass accelerates and it rotates with increasing angular speed.
questions.explanation: The net force is zero, so the center of mass does not accelerate. The two forces produce torques in the same rotational direction about the center, so the net torque is not zero and the rod's angular speed increases.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping down the ramp shown. Which of the following describes the friction force exerted on the ball by the ramp?
choices: It is kinetic friction directed up the ramp, and it dissipates part of the ball's energy.
It is static friction directed down the ramp, and it increases the ball's speed.
It is static friction directed up the ramp, and it provides the torque that increases the ball's rate of rotation.
It is zero, because the point of contact does not slide.
questions.explanation: As the ball speeds up it must also spin faster, which requires a torque about its center; gravity and the normal force exert none. Friction directed up the ramp supplies that torque. Because the point of contact does not slide, the friction is static and dissipates no energy.

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere is released from rest at the top of a ramp of height \(h\) and rolls without slipping, as shown. The rotational inertia of the sphere is \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\). What is the speed of the center of the sphere at the bottom of the ramp?
questions.explanation: Energy conservation with \(\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}\) gives \(Mgh=\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac{7}{10}Mv^2\). The speed is less than \(\sqrt{2gh}\) because part of the energy is rotational.

questions.stem: A hoop, a solid disk, and a solid sphere are released from rest at the top of the ramp shown and roll without slipping. The objects have different masses and radii. Which of the following correctly predicts the order in which they reach the bottom?
choices: Hoop, then disk, then sphere, regardless of their masses and radii
The object with the smallest mass arrives first.
They arrive together, because all objects fall with the same acceleration.
Sphere, then disk, then hoop, regardless of their masses and radii
questions.explanation: For rolling without slipping, the acceleration depends only on how the mass is distributed, through the factor \(\dfrac{I}{MR^2}\): \(\tfrac{2}{5}\) for the sphere, \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) for the disk, and \(1\) for the hoop. The smaller that fraction, the smaller the share of energy that goes into rotation and the faster the object travels.

questions.stem: A ball rolls without slipping along a horizontal floor and then moves up a ramp. In trial 1 the ramp is rough enough that the ball rolls without slipping. In trial 2 the ramp is frictionless. How do the maximum heights the ball reaches compare?
choices: It rises higher in trial 2, because no energy is dissipated by friction.
It rises higher in trial 1, because its rotational kinetic energy is also converted to potential energy.
The heights are equal, because the ball has the same total kinetic energy at the bottom.
It rises higher in trial 2, because friction opposes the motion in trial 1.
questions.explanation: On the frictionless ramp nothing exerts a torque on the ball, so it keeps spinning at the same rate and only its translational kinetic energy becomes potential energy. On the rough ramp static friction, which dissipates no energy, slows the rotation, so all of the kinetic energy is converted.

questions.stem: A skater spinning on frictionless ice pulls her arms in, reducing her rotational inertia to one third of its original value. By what factor does her rotational kinetic energy change?
choices: It increases by a factor of 3.
It increases by a factor of 9.
It decreases by a factor of 3.
questions.explanation: Angular momentum \(I\omega\) is conserved, so her angular speed triples. Rotational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\), so reducing \(I\) to one third triples the energy. The skater does work in pulling her arms inward.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) spins freely with angular speed \(\omega_0\) about a vertical axle through its center. A thin ring of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), initially not rotating, is dropped onto the disk so that their centers coincide, and friction brings them to a common angular speed. The rotational inertia of the disk is \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\) and that of the ring is \(MR^2\). What is the final angular speed?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: \(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\omega_0=\left(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2+MR^2\right)\omega\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{\omega_0}{3}\). Assuming kinetic energy is conserved instead gives \(\dfrac{\omega_0}{\sqrt{3}}\), but the friction between the surfaces dissipates energy.

questions.stem: A child stands at the rim of a merry-go-round that rotates freely on a frictionless axle. The child walks to the center. For the system of the child and the merry-go-round, which of the following describes the changes in angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy?
choices: The angular momentum stays the same and the kinetic energy increases.
The angular momentum and the kinetic energy both stay the same.
The angular momentum increases and the kinetic energy stays the same.
The angular momentum stays the same and the kinetic energy decreases.
questions.explanation: No external torque acts, so the angular momentum is constant. The rotational inertia decreases, so the angular speed increases, and the kinetic energy \(\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\) increases. The additional energy comes from the work the child does in walking inward.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit around a planet. Its speed is \(v\) at its closest point, a distance \(r\) from the planet's center. What is its speed at its farthest point, a distance \(4r\) from the planet's center?
questions.explanation: The gravitational force points toward the planet and exerts no torque about it, so the satellite's angular momentum is conserved. At the closest and farthest points the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so \(mvr=mv'(4r)\) and \(v'=\dfrac{v}{4}\).

questions.stem: A uniform rod of mass \(M\) and length \(L\) lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface and can rotate about a fixed pivot at one end. A lump of clay of mass \(m\) moving with speed \(v\) perpendicular to the rod strikes the free end and sticks, as shown. The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is \(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2\). What is the angular speed of the rod just after the collision?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about the pivot is conserved: \(mvL=\left(\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2+mL^2\right)\omega\). Solving gives \(\omega=\dfrac{3mv}{(M+3m)L}\).

questions.stem: A lump of clay strikes and sticks to the free end of a rod that can rotate about a fixed pivot at its other end, as shown. For the system of the clay and the rod, which quantities are conserved during the collision?
choices: Linear momentum and angular momentum about the pivot
Angular momentum about the pivot only
Linear momentum, angular momentum about the pivot, and kinetic energy
questions.explanation: The pivot exerts an external force on the rod during the collision, so linear momentum is not conserved. That force acts at the pivot, so it exerts no torque about the pivot and angular momentum about that point is conserved. Kinetic energy is dissipated because the clay sticks.

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere, with rotational inertia \(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), rolls without slipping along a horizontal surface. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
questions.explanation: With \(\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}\), the rotational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\dfrac{v^2}{R^2}=\tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2\) and the translational kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2\). The rotational fraction is \(\dfrac{1/5}{7/10}=\dfrac{2}{7}\).

questions.stem: A flywheel with rotational inertia \(3.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) starts from rest and is acted on by a constant net torque of \(6.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) as it turns through \(25\text{ rad}\). What is its final angular speed?
questions.explanation: The work done by the torque is \(\tau\,\Delta\theta=150\text{ J}\). Setting this equal to \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\) gives \(\omega^2=100\), so \(\omega=10\text{ rad/s}\).

questions.stem: A wheel is initially at rest on a frictionless axle. A net torque of \(4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) acts on it for \(3.0\text{ s}\), followed immediately by a net torque of \(2.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) in the opposite direction for \(2.0\text{ s}\). What is the magnitude of the wheel's angular momentum at the end of the \(5.0\text{ s}\)?
questions.explanation: The change in angular momentum equals the angular impulse, the net torque multiplied by the time it acts: \(4.0(3.0)-2.0(2.0)=8.0\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\text{/s}\). The rotational inertia is not needed.

questions.stem: A solid sphere and a hoop of equal mass are released from rest at the top of the ramp shown and roll without slipping. How do their kinetic energies compare at the bottom?
choices: Their total kinetic energies are equal, and the sphere has more translational kinetic energy.
Their total kinetic energies are equal, and so are their translational kinetic energies.
The sphere has more total kinetic energy, because it is moving faster.
The hoop has more total kinetic energy, because it has more rotational inertia.
questions.explanation: Each object converts the same potential energy \(mgh\) into kinetic energy, so the totals are equal. The hoop puts half of its kinetic energy into rotation and the sphere only two sevenths, so the sphere has more translational kinetic energy and reaches the bottom moving faster.

questions.stem: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elongated elliptical orbit. Where in its orbit is the comet moving fastest, and why?
choices: At its farthest point from the Sun, because the gravitational force on it is weakest there.
At its closest point to the Sun, because the Sun exerts a torque that speeds it up there.
Its speed is the same everywhere, because the mechanical energy of the comet–Sun system is constant.
At its closest point to the Sun, because its angular momentum about the Sun is constant and its distance is smallest there.
questions.explanation: The gravitational force points along the line to the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and the comet's angular momentum is conserved. A smaller distance therefore requires a greater speed. Equivalently, the system's potential energy is lowest at the closest point, so the kinetic energy is highest.

questions.stem: A student sits at rest on a stool that can rotate freely about a vertical axis. The student holds a wheel with its axle vertical; the wheel is spinning counterclockwise as seen from above. The student turns the wheel over so that it spins clockwise as seen from above. What happens to the student and the stool?
choices: They rotate clockwise, with an angular momentum equal to the wheel's original angular momentum.
They rotate counterclockwise, with an angular momentum equal to twice the wheel's original angular momentum.
They rotate counterclockwise, with an angular momentum equal to the wheel's original angular momentum.
They remain at rest, because the wheel's angular speed has not changed.
questions.explanation: No external torque acts about the vertical axis, so the total angular momentum stays equal to the wheel's original value \(L\), counterclockwise. After the flip the wheel has \(-L\), so the student and stool must have \(+2L\) for the total to remain \(L\).

questions.stem: A lump of clay strikes the free end of a pivoted rod and sticks, as shown, giving the rod an angular speed \(\omega\). The experiment is repeated with a rubber ball of the same mass and speed, which bounces straight back. How does the rod's angular speed just after the collision compare with \(\omega\)?
choices: It is smaller, because the ball does not stay with the rod.
It is greater, because the ball's angular momentum about the pivot changes by a larger amount.
It is the same, because the ball and the clay have the same angular momentum before the collision.
It is smaller, because the ball keeps some kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: The total angular momentum about the pivot is conserved. The clay ends up with a small angular momentum in its original direction, while the ball's angular momentum reverses direction, so the ball's change is larger and the rod receives more angular momentum.

questions.stem: A bowling ball is released onto a rough horizontal lane sliding at speed \(v\) without rotating. Which of the following describes its motion afterward?
choices: Its speed and its rate of rotation both decrease until it stops.
Its speed stays constant while its rate of rotation increases.
Its speed decreases until it stops, and then it begins to roll.
Its speed decreases and its rate of rotation increases until it rolls without slipping, and then both remain constant.
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction acts backward at the point of contact, which slows the ball's center and also exerts a torque that spins the ball up. Once the speed of the center equals \(R\omega\), the contact point no longer slides, the kinetic friction disappears, and the ball rolls at constant speed.

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. What is the maximum speed of the block?
questions.explanation: The amplitude is \(A=0.20\text{ m}\) and the period is \(T=2.0\text{ s}\), so \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\pi\text{ rad/s}\). The maximum speed is \(A\omega=0.20\pi\approx 0.63\text{ m/s}\). The average speed over a cycle is \(\dfrac{4A}{T}=0.40\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. Which of the following describes the block's velocity and acceleration at \(t=0.5\text{ s}\)?
choices: The velocity is zero; the acceleration has its maximum magnitude and is negative.
The velocity and the acceleration are both zero.
The velocity has its maximum magnitude and is negative; the acceleration is zero.
The velocity has its maximum magnitude and is positive; the acceleration is zero.
questions.explanation: At \(t=0.5\text{ s}\) the block passes through equilibrium, where the graph is steepest and sloping downward, so the velocity is most negative. The restoring force, and therefore the acceleration, is zero at equilibrium.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) attached to a spring of spring constant \(k\) oscillates on a frictionless surface with period \(T\), as shown. The block is replaced with one of mass \(2m\), and the spring is replaced with one of spring constant \(\dfrac{k}{2}\). What is the new period?
questions.explanation: The period is \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\). Doubling the mass and halving the spring constant multiplies \(\dfrac{m}{k}\) by 4, so the period doubles.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\) on a frictionless surface, as shown. The block is then set oscillating with amplitude \(2A\). How do the period, the maximum speed, and the total mechanical energy change?
choices: The period doubles, the maximum speed is unchanged, and the energy doubles.
The period is unchanged, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy doubles.
The period is unchanged, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy quadruples.
The period doubles, the maximum speed doubles, and the energy quadruples.
questions.explanation: The period of a spring–block oscillator depends only on mass and spring constant, not on amplitude. The total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\), so it quadruples, and since that equals \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2\), the maximum speed doubles.

questions.explanation: At \(x=\dfrac{A}{2}\) the potential energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}k\left(\tfrac{A}{2}\right)^2\), one fourth of the total, so the kinetic energy is three fourths of its maximum. Speed depends on the square root of kinetic energy, giving \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v_{\max}\).

questions.explanation: The period is \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\). Multiplying both the length and the field strength by 4 leaves \(\dfrac{L}{g}\) unchanged, so the period is the same.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum swings with a small amplitude, as shown. The bob is replaced with one of twice the mass, and the pendulum is released from twice the original angle, still a small angle. How does the period compare with the original period?
choices: It is longer by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).
questions.explanation: For small angles the period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length and the gravitational field strength. A greater mass increases the restoring force and the inertia in the same proportion, and a larger small amplitude means a greater distance covered at a proportionally greater speed.

questions.stem: When a block is hung from a vertical spring, the spring stretches a distance \(d\) before the block hangs at rest. The block is then pulled down slightly and released. What is the period of its oscillation?
choices: It cannot be determined without the mass of the block.
questions.explanation: At equilibrium \(kd=mg\), so \(\dfrac{m}{k}=\dfrac{d}{g}\). Substituting into \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\) gives \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{d}{g}}\); the mass and spring constant are not needed separately.

questions.stem: A block of mass \(m\) on a spring oscillates with amplitude \(A\) on a frictionless horizontal surface. At the instant the block passes through its equilibrium position, a lump of clay of mass \(m\) is dropped vertically onto the block and sticks. What is the amplitude of the oscillation afterward?
questions.explanation: Horizontal momentum is conserved as the clay lands, so the speed at equilibrium is halved while the mass doubles. The kinetic energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2m)\left(\tfrac{v}{2}\right)^2\) is half its previous value. Since the total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2\), halving the energy reduces the amplitude by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\).

questions.stem: A \(0.50\text{ kg}\) block on a spring with spring constant \(200\text{ N/m}\) oscillates on a frictionless horizontal surface with amplitude \(0.10\text{ m}\). What is the speed of the block when it is \(0.060\text{ m}\) from equilibrium?
questions.explanation: The total energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(200)(0.10)^2=1.0\text{ J}\). At \(0.060\text{ m}\) the potential energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(200)(0.060)^2=0.36\text{ J}\), leaving \(0.64\text{ J}\) of kinetic energy, so \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.64)}{0.50}}=1.6\text{ m/s}\). The maximum speed is \(2.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A simple pendulum and a block on a vertical spring both oscillate inside an elevator. The elevator begins to accelerate upward at a constant rate. How do the periods of the two oscillators change?
choices: The pendulum's period decreases and the spring–block period is unchanged.
The pendulum's period is unchanged and the spring–block period decreases.
questions.explanation: In the upward-accelerating elevator, objects behave as if the gravitational field strength were \(g+a\). The pendulum's period \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g+a}}\) decreases. The spring–block period \(2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\) does not depend on \(g\); only the equilibrium position shifts.

questions.stem: A block is attached to two identical springs. When the springs are connected side by side (in parallel), the block oscillates with period \(T_p\). When the springs are connected end to end (in series), it oscillates with period \(T_s\). What is \(\dfrac{T_s}{T_p}\)?
questions.explanation: In parallel the effective spring constant is \(2k\); in series it is \(\dfrac{k}{2}\). The period is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}}}\), so \(\dfrac{T_s}{T_p}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2k}{k/2}}=2\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the position of a block oscillating on a spring as a function of time. At which of the following times is the kinetic energy of the block greatest?
questions.explanation: The block moves fastest as it passes through equilibrium, \(x=0\), where the graph is steepest; that happens at \(t=1.5\text{ s}\). At the other times listed the block is at maximum displacement, momentarily at rest, with all of the energy stored in the spring.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates between \(x=-A\) and \(x=+A\) on a frictionless surface, as shown. Which of the following is true at the instant the block is at \(x=+A\)?
choices: Its velocity and its acceleration are both zero.
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its greatest magnitude and is directed away from \(x=0\).
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its greatest magnitude and is directed toward \(x=0\).
Its velocity has its greatest magnitude and its acceleration is zero.
questions.explanation: At the turning point the block is momentarily at rest, but the spring is stretched the most, so the restoring force and the acceleration are greatest and point back toward equilibrium. If the acceleration were zero there, the block would stay at rest.

questions.stem: A block on a spring is released from rest at \(x=+A\), as shown. How does the time it takes to move from \(x=+A\) to \(x=\tfrac{A}{2}\) compare with the time it takes to move from \(x=\tfrac{A}{2}\) to \(x=0\)?
choices: The two intervals are equal, because the distances are equal.
The first interval is shorter, because the acceleration is greatest near the turning point.
The two intervals are equal, because the period does not depend on amplitude.
The first interval is longer, because the block is moving more slowly near the turning point.
questions.explanation: The block starts from rest at \(x=+A\) and is still slow as it reaches \(\tfrac{A}{2}\), while it covers the second half of the distance near its maximum speed. With \(x=A\cos\omega t\), the first interval lasts one sixth of a period and the second lasts one twelfth.

questions.stem: A block on a spring oscillates with period \(T\). Which of the following describes how the kinetic energy of the block varies with time?
choices: It oscillates between zero and a maximum with period \(T\).
It oscillates between negative and positive values with period \(T\).
It oscillates between zero and a maximum with period \(\dfrac{T}{2}\).
It remains constant, because mechanical energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: The block passes through equilibrium, where its kinetic energy is greatest, twice in each cycle, once in each direction. Kinetic energy depends on the square of the velocity, so it is never negative and it repeats twice as often as the position does.

questions.stem: Water of density \(\rho\) flows through the horizontal pipe shown. The cross-sectional area at section 1 is four times the area at section 2, and the speed of the water at section 1 is \(v\). What is the pressure at section 1 minus the pressure at section 2?
questions.explanation: Continuity gives a speed of \(4v\) at section 2. Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe gives \(P_1-P_2=\tfrac{1}{2}\rho\left[(4v)^2-v^2\right]=\dfrac{15}{2}\rho v^2\). The pressure is higher where the water moves more slowly.

choices: The pressure is lower at section 2, because a net force toward section 2 is needed to speed the water up as it enters the narrow section.
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the water is squeezed into a smaller space.
The pressure is the same at both sections, because the pipe is horizontal.
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the water there is moving faster and pushes harder on the walls.
questions.explanation: The water must speed up to pass through the narrow section at the same volume flow rate. An element of water entering the constriction accelerates forward, so the pressure behind it must be greater than the pressure ahead of it.

questions.stem: Water streams from a small hole in the side of a large open tank filled to height \(H\), as shown. At what depth \(h\) below the water surface should the hole be made so that the stream lands as far from the tank as possible?
choices: As close to the bottom of the tank as possible
As close to the water surface as possible
questions.explanation: The water leaves with speed \(\sqrt{2gh}\) and falls for a time \(\sqrt{\dfrac{2(H-h)}{g}}\), so it lands a distance \(2\sqrt{h(H-h)}\) away. That product is greatest when \(h=\dfrac{H}{2}\). A lower hole gives a faster stream but too little time to fall.

questions.stem: Water streams from a small hole in the side of a large open tank, as shown. The hole is \(0.80\text{ m}\) below the water surface. Using \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\), what is the speed of the water as it leaves the hole?
questions.explanation: Applying Bernoulli's equation between the surface, where the water is nearly at rest, and the hole, both at atmospheric pressure, gives \(v=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2(10)(0.80)}=4.0\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A block floats in water of density \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\) with three fourths of its volume submerged, as shown. The block is then placed in oil of density \(900\text{ kg/m}^3\). What fraction of the block's volume is submerged in the oil?
questions.explanation: A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid, so the submerged fraction equals the ratio of the object's density to the fluid's density. The block's density is \(750\text{ kg/m}^3\), so in oil the fraction is \(\dfrac{750}{900}=\dfrac{5}{6}\).

questions.stem: A boat carrying a heavy steel anchor floats in a small pond. The anchor is thrown overboard and sinks to the bottom. What happens to the water level of the pond?
choices: It rises, because the anchor now displaces water directly.
It falls, because the sunken anchor displaces less water than it did while it was in the boat.
It stays the same, because the total mass in the pond has not changed.
It rises, because the boat floats higher after the anchor is removed.
questions.explanation: While in the boat, the anchor causes the boat to displace a volume of water equal in weight to the anchor, which is much larger than the anchor's own volume because steel is denser than water. On the bottom it displaces only its own volume, so the total displaced volume decreases.

questions.stem: An object weighs \(30\text{ N}\) in air. When it is completely submerged in water of density \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\) and suspended from a spring scale, the scale reads \(20\text{ N}\). What is the density of the object?
questions.explanation: The buoyant force is \(30-20=10\text{ N}\), which is the weight of a volume of water equal to the object's volume. The object weighs three times as much as that water, so it is three times as dense.

questions.stem: Three open containers with different shapes have bases of equal area and are filled with water to the same height. One has vertical sides, one widens toward the top, and one narrows toward the top. How do the forces exerted by the water on the bases of the containers compare?
choices: The force is greatest in the container that widens, because it holds the most water.
The force is greatest in the container that narrows, because the water is compressed.
The force equals the weight of the water in each container, so all three are different.
They are equal, because the pressure at the base depends only on the depth of the water.
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure at depth \(h\) is \(\rho gh\) whatever the shape of the container, and the bases have equal areas, so the forces are equal. In the containers with slanted sides, the walls exert vertical forces on the water that account for the difference between that force and the water's weight.

questions.stem: In a hydraulic lift, the area of the large piston is 20 times the area of the small piston. The fluid is incompressible. How far must the small piston be pushed down to raise a car on the large piston by \(0.10\text{ m}\)?
questions.explanation: The volume of fluid pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume that enters the large one, so \(A_sd_s=A_Ld_L\) and \(d_s=20(0.10)=2.0\text{ m}\). The force is multiplied by 20, but the work done is the same on both sides.

questions.stem: A diver is \(20\text{ m}\) below the surface of a lake. The density of the water is \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\), atmospheric pressure is \(1.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\), and \(g=10\text{ m/s}^2\). What is the absolute pressure at the diver's depth?
questions.explanation: The gauge pressure is \(\rho gh=1000(10)(20)=2.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\). The absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure, for \(3.0\times 10^5\text{ Pa}\).

questions.stem: A block of wood with density \(500\text{ kg/m}^3\) is held at rest by a string attached to the bottom of a tank of water, with the block completely submerged. The density of water is \(1000\text{ kg/m}^3\). The string is cut. Neglecting drag, what is the acceleration of the block immediately afterward?
choices: Zero, because the block was in equilibrium
questions.explanation: The buoyant force is \(\rho_{\text{water}}Vg\), twice the block's weight \(\rho_{\text{wood}}Vg\). The net force is therefore equal to the weight and directed upward, giving an acceleration of \(g\) upward. Before the cut, the string supplied a downward force equal to the block's weight.

questions.stem: Water flows at \(2.0\text{ m/s}\) through a hose of radius \(1.0\text{ cm}\) and leaves through a nozzle of radius \(0.25\text{ cm}\). What is the speed of the water as it leaves the nozzle?
questions.explanation: The volume flow rate \(Av\) is constant. The radius decreases by a factor of 4, so the area decreases by a factor of 16 and the speed increases by a factor of 16, to \(32\text{ m/s}\).

questions.stem: A block floats in fresh water, as shown. The block is then placed in salt water, which is denser than fresh water. How do the buoyant force on the block and the volume of the block that is submerged compare with their values in fresh water?
choices: The buoyant force is greater and the submerged volume is the same.
The buoyant force is the same and the submerged volume is smaller.
The buoyant force is greater and the submerged volume is smaller.
The buoyant force is the same and the submerged volume is the same.
questions.explanation: A floating block is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force equals the block's weight in either liquid. The buoyant force also equals the weight of the displaced liquid, and a smaller volume of the denser liquid has that weight.

figure.alt: An open tank filled with water to height H above the ground. Water streams from a small hole in the side at depth h below the surface and lands on the ground

questions.stem: A large open tank is filled with water to height \(H\), as shown. One small hole is made at depth \(h\) below the surface, and a second small hole is made at height \(h\) above the ground. How do the horizontal distances at which the two streams land compare?
choices: The stream from the lower hole lands farther away, because it leaves with a greater speed.
The stream from the upper hole lands farther away, because it falls for a longer time.
The answer depends on whether \(h\) is less than or greater than \(\dfrac{H}{2}\).
questions.explanation: A stream from depth \(d\) leaves with speed \(\sqrt{2gd}\) and falls for a time \(\sqrt{2(H-d)/g}\), so it lands \(2\sqrt{d(H-d)}\) away. Depths of \(h\) and \(H-h\) give the same product: the upper stream is slower but falls longer by exactly the compensating amount.

questions.stem: A solid metal cube hangs from a string and is completely submerged in a tank of water. The cube is lowered until it is twice as deep, still without touching the bottom. Treating water as incompressible, how does the tension in the string change?
choices: It decreases, because the pressure on the cube is greater at the greater depth.
It increases, because more water lies above the cube.
It stays the same, because the buoyant force depends on the volume of water displaced, not on depth.
It decreases, because the buoyant force is proportional to depth.
questions.explanation: The pressures on the top and bottom faces both increase with depth, but their difference, which produces the buoyant force, depends only on the height of the cube. The buoyant force and the cube's weight are unchanged, so the tension is unchanged.

questions.stem: A beaker of water sits on a scale. A student lowers a finger into the water without touching the beaker, and no water spills. What happens to the reading on the scale?
choices: It increases by an amount equal to the buoyant force on the finger.
It stays the same, because the finger is supported by the student and does not touch the beaker.
It increases by an amount equal to the weight of the finger.
It decreases, because the water exerts an upward force on the finger.
questions.explanation: The water exerts an upward buoyant force on the finger, so by Newton's third law the finger exerts an equal downward force on the water, and that force is passed on to the scale. Equivalently, the water level rises, increasing the pressure on the bottom of the beaker.
